pr_title: Fix cache_clear behaviour in all fixtures and tests
pr_body:
When running test with pytest-xdist, tests can be executed in random order in multiple workers. This means that if a test leaves a side-effect, it might affect another test - much more easily, because you are not able to rely on the sequence of test execution.

The `recalculate_patterns` fixture in "test_serde" had such a side effect and caused #35699 to happen.

It was used in order to clear the cache BEFORE the test so that it could reload the patterns using different configugration provided by the test as new configuration.

The side effect of it was however such, that after the test completed, the new configuration remained in the cache AFTER the test has been completed - thus if THE SAME xdist worker started ANOTHER test that relied on the cache containting "regular" value (and it did not use the same fixtuere to clean it), it - surpisingly - got the value that was read from the special configuration provided by the previous test.

This PR fixes it by clearing the cache also AFTER the test has completed, which means that any other test running in the same worker will refresh the test again - with the configuration it is supposed to have. This is done with try/finally pattern, because context manager / yield will not execute the post-yield code when an exception is thrown, so if there is a failed assertion, the cache_clear afer yield might not happen and such `cache_clear` test that fails might still cause cache pollution.

Fixes: #35699

pr_comments:
Very insteresting finding :). It took me a while to figure out the exact scenario where https://github.com/apache/airflow/issues/35699 could have happen -but I believe this one perfectly explains it.

cc: @bolkedebruin
Cliché, but yet another proof that  `Cache invalidation is the most .....`
Ah indeed, I was wondering how the pollution could happen at all. I wasn't aware of pytest-xdist. It feels to me like a bug in pytest-xdist, but this is a good fix.

> Ah indeed, I was wondering how the pollution could happen at all. I wasn't aware of pytest-xdist. It feels to me like a bug in pytest-xdist, but this is a good fix.

Just to explain. It's not bug in pytest nor pytest-xdist, It was OUR bug in OUR fixtures coming from lack of understanding that this kind of change has side effects in global shared state which is reused between tests run with pytest (or pytest-xdist). So it's not a "good" fix. It's proper way of writing such fixtures.

It's not exclusive to `pytest-xdist`. This is the same for any other pytest execution - simply in pytest-xdist you are less reliant on specific execution sequence of the tests - so it is just more likely to happen in a flaky way. When you run things in a single `pytest` command - the execution sequence of the test is deterministic (alphabetical sequence of packages,  modules, test classes and tests) - which means that you might never found out you had the problem (in case of https://github.com/apache/airflow/issues/35699 the thing was that the last test case in the test suite for serde did not have special configuratin but it DID have the fixture applied - so it re-read the cache from "original" configiuration - thus any tests that were run before or after had "no pollution" (but this was accidental).

Simply the fact that pytest-xdist i slightly less deterministic revealed the problem - but it's not "pytest-xdist" bug. It's just the way how tests work - generally in Pytest (and most other test frameworks) tests are run in the same python interpreter, one after the other - so such cache pollution might happen (this is what for example pytest-antilru goal is to remove that side effect - it attempts to remove the cache altogether so that side effects are not carried through other tests. But it either has bugs or we have other side effects because when I turn it on it breaks few tests (did not have time to take a look).

If you would like to avoid (some, not all) side effects you would have to really fork every single test method to separate python interpreter and do it before any other initialization of any other python packages happen - but that would be very, very slow (3000 tests * (even) 0.1 s fork = 300 seconds - but that does not include the time for initialization of other package/iimports). Also it does not remove all side-effects, for example you can store global state in disk or shared memory or shared state might be present in the form of spawned/forked other processes etc. ec.  There are plenty of other way you can have global shared state that some tests implicitly rely on but some other tests are changing that state and they do not clean-up after themselves (as they should). In this case pytest (and other test frameworks of this kind) leave the responsibility with cleaning/restoring the shared global state to the tests (this is what setup/teardown and pytest fixtures are supposed to do).

So while the setting where it all runs in a single interpreter  (or in case of pytest-xdist - in several python interpreters that run in parallel) is  not perfect (it cannot be) it's also "good enough" balance between speed and isolation in most cases as long as you remember to not modify (or if you remember to restore) shared global state in the tests.

In our case it was evidently a bug in our fixtures implementation - not in pytest, nor in pytest-xdist. Simply, it violates the (implicit) agreement that when you change global state in tests that other tests might rely on, we should restore that global state after the test. In this case - we changed shared global state of the cache and we did not restore it properly. That was our bug not pytest, nor pytest-xdist. It comes from not understanding the side effect such shared global state might have. Most of flaky test are result of similar bugs.

BTW. I am actually planning - this is the best practice for flaky tests and stability - to run the tests in randomized order  https://pypi.org/project/pytest-random-order/ is one of the plugins -  initially for NonDB tests. It is however a bit problematic, because when you randomize the tests then any PR might introduce a side effect that will only be visible when you run the tests in other order, so it's a bit tricky to get right, but it has the potential to uncover and tame the flaky tests we currently have. The nice thing about those random order plugins is that when they fail, you can run them with the same seed when the tests failed, that increases the chances of reproducing the flaky tests (but combined with pytest-xdist it also add some randomness due to parallell/distributed execution).

For those who are interested - I heartily recommend that recent podcast from Talk Python To me - "Tamiing Flaky tests" - where a lot of that is explained and there are some interesting techniques (which I am gradually employing) on how to deal with the flaky tests  https://talkpython.fm/episodes/show/429/taming-flaky-tests

issue_context.title: Flaky TestSerializers.test_params test
issue_context.body:
### Body

Recently we started to have a flaky TestSerializers.test_params

This seems to be a problem in either the tests or implementation of `serde`  - seems like discovery of classes that are serializable in some cases is not working well while the import of serde happens.

It happens rarely and it's not easy to reproduce locallly, by a quick look it might be a side effect from another test - I have a feeling that when tests are run, some other test might leave behind a thread that cleans the list of classes that have been registered with serde and that cleanup happens somewhat randomly. 

cc: @bolkedebruin - maybe you can take a look or have an idea where it can come from - might be fastest for you as you know the discovery mechanism best and you wrote most of the tests there ? Maybe there are some specially crafted test cases somewhere that do a setup/teardown or just cleanup of the serde-registered classes that could cause such an effect?

Example error:  https://github.com/apache/airflow/actions/runs/6898122803/job/18767848684?pr=35693#step:5:754


Error:

```

[gw3] linux -- Python 3.8.18 /usr/local/bin/python

self = <tests.serialization.serializers.test_serializers.TestSerializers object at 0x7fb113165550>

    def test_params(self):
        i = ParamsDict({"x": Param(default="value", description="there is a value", key="test")})
        e = serialize(i)
>       d = deserialize(e)

tests/serialization/serializers/test_serializers.py:173:

o = {'__classname__': 'airflow.models.param.ParamsDict', '__data__': {'x': 'value'}, '__version__': 1}
full = True, type_hint = None

    def deserialize(o: T | None, full=True, type_hint: Any = None) -> object:
        """
        Deserialize an object of primitive type and uses an allow list to determine if a class can be loaded.
    
        :param o: primitive to deserialize into an arbitrary object.
        :param full: if False it will return a stringified representation
                     of an object and will not load any classes
        :param type_hint: if set it will be used to help determine what
                     object to deserialize in. It does not override if another
                     specification is found
        :return: object
        """
        if o is None:
            return o
    
        if isinstance(o, _primitives):
            return o
    
        # tuples, sets are included here for backwards compatibility
        if isinstance(o, _builtin_collections):
            col = [deserialize(d) for d in o]
            if isinstance(o, tuple):
                return tuple(col)
    
            if isinstance(o, set):
                return set(col)
    
            return col
    
        if not isinstance(o, dict):
            # if o is not a dict, then it's already deserialized
            # in this case we should return it as is
            return o
    
        o = _convert(o)
    
        # plain dict and no type hint
        if CLASSNAME not in o and not type_hint or VERSION not in o:
            return {str(k): deserialize(v, full) for k, v in o.items()}
    
        # custom deserialization starts here
        cls: Any
        version = 0
        value: Any = None
        classname = ""
    
        if type_hint:
            cls = type_hint
            classname = qualname(cls)
            version = 0  # type hinting always sets version to 0
            value = o
    
        if CLASSNAME in o and VERSION in o:
            classname, version, value = decode(o)
    
        if not classname:
            raise TypeError("classname cannot be empty")
    
        # only return string representation
        if not full:
            return _stringify(classname, version, value)
    
        if not _match(classname) and classname not in _extra_allowed:
>           raise ImportError(
                f"{classname} was not found in allow list for deserialization imports. "
                f"To allow it, add it to allowed_deserialization_classes in the configuration"
            )
E           ImportError: airflow.models.param.ParamsDict was not found in allow list for deserialization imports. To allow it, add it to allowed_deserialization_classes in the configuration

airflow/serialization/serde.py:246: ImportError
```

comments: Looking. First glance: `Param` does have its own `serialize` method, so there is _no_ discover issue at hand here. The error message does give a hint though where the issue might be. The `allowed_deserialization_classes` in `[core]` is checked for what patterns of classnames are allowed to be deserialized. Typically this contains "airflow.*". The patterns are cached. So i wonder what happens with the setting of `allowed_deserialization_classes` - empty? this is probably where the issue is, and if not, what is in the cache?

>  this is probably where the issue is, and if not, what is in the cache?

Welll. again the case where `cache invalidation is the most difficult ....` :)

review_comments: Super interesting pattern and the reasoning for it :D
